Value at risk is not a maximum loss: compare the quantile with expected shortfall

Use one original five-state return model to distinguish a loss threshold, the average of an exact worst tail and the largest specified loss, including probability mass at a boundary.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 6 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Inspect an invented five-state loss distribution and its exact upper-tail measures

Interactive planning lab

Loss quantile at 95% cumulative probability (VaR)$5,000
Average loss in the worst 5% of model probability (ES)$24,000
Largest loss among the five invented outcomes$40,000

Original, completely specified one-year probability model with five mutually exclusive outcomes. Baseline simple returns are −40%, −20%, −5%, +5% and +12%, with assumed probabilities 1%, 4%, 15%, 40% and 40%. The scale changes only the three loss sizes; gain outcomes and all probabilities remain fixed. These are chosen numbers, not market observations, estimated frequencies or forecasts. Positive loss means a decline; negative loss means a gain. VaR is the smallest loss value whose cumulative probability is at least the selected level, with no floor at zero. ES averages exactly the worst remaining probability mass, taking only the needed fraction of a boundary state. Confidence here is a cumulative model probability, not a statistical confidence interval. No normality, sample, p-value, simulation, serial returns, leverage, fees, taxes, cash flows or regulatory-capital calculation is used. The largest modeled loss is only a bound of these five invented outcomes and is not an actual investment’s maximum loss. These risk summaries do not determine a sufficient cash reserve or the probability of meeting a household goal.

  1. Begin with an explicit distribution rather than an unexplained risk number

The central idea

A quantile says where a cumulative probability threshold is reached. It does not describe how large worse losses can be. Expected shortfall adds tail severity, but still depends on the stated model.

01

Begin with an explicit distribution rather than an unexplained risk number

A value-at-risk figure can be mistaken for the most money an investment could lose. To see why that interpretation fails, write down the possible outcomes and their probabilities before calculating the summary.

This example has exactly five one-year returns: −40% with probability 1%, −20% with probability 4%, −5% with probability 15%, +5% with probability 40% and +12% with probability 40%. These numbers are invented and fully specify the model. They are not a market sample, a backtest or a forecast for any asset.

For CAD 100,000 of opening capital, the corresponding loss values are CAD 40,000, CAD 20,000, CAD 5,000, negative CAD 5,000 and negative CAD 12,000. Positive loss represents money lost; negative loss represents a gain.

The probability bars show the assumed frequency weight of each complete outcome. They do not show loss size through bar length. All five states are mutually exclusive, and their probabilities sum to 100%.

02

Specify which loss quantile the value-at-risk number represents

The calculator defines VaR at cumulative level α as the smallest loss value for which the probability of a loss at or below that value is at least α. This fixes the treatment of the boundaries in a discrete distribution.

At the default 95% level, both gain states contribute 80% of probability. Including the CAD 5,000 loss state adds another 15%, reaching 95%. The defined 95% VaR is therefore CAD 5,000.

The remaining 5% of model probability still contains CAD 20,000 and CAD 40,000 losses. CAD 5,000 is consequently not the largest possible loss even inside this small invented distribution. It identifies a cumulative threshold.

The word confidence here refers to that selected model probability. It is not a 95% statistical confidence interval estimated from observations, and the example provides no evidence that a real portfolio has those probabilities.

03

Average the losses inside the selected worst tail

Expected shortfall, abbreviated ES, averages the losses in exactly the worst probability tail corresponding to the selected level. At 95%, that tail contains the worst 5% of model probability.

The CAD 40,000 loss has probability 1%, and the CAD 20,000 loss has probability 4%. Their combined probability is exactly 5%. Within that tail, their weights are 1 ÷ 5 = 20% and 4 ÷ 5 = 80%.

The average is 0.2 × CAD 40,000 + 0.8 × CAD 20,000 = CAD 24,000. The waterfall shows CAD 8,000 and CAD 16,000 contributions to this average. It does not add both full losses as if two mutually exclusive outcomes occurred together.

ES is still not a maximum: the CAD 40,000 outcome exceeds the CAD 24,000 tail average. Both the quantile and the average lose information compared with the complete distribution.

04

Take only the probability mass needed at the boundary

Change the cumulative level to 90%. VaR remains CAD 5,000 because the cumulative probability jumps from 80% to 95% at that loss. There is no state that makes the cumulative total exactly 90%.

The worst tail now needs 10% of probability. The two larger-loss states supply 5%. The remaining 5% comes from the 15%-probability CAD 5,000 state. This uses one-third of that state’s probability mass for the tail calculation.

The resulting average is (1% × CAD 40,000 + 4% × CAD 20,000 + 5% × CAD 5,000) ÷ 10% = CAD 14,500. Simply averaging states strictly worse than VaR would instead use only 5% of probability and produce CAD 24,000, answering a different question.

Taking every state at or above VaR would use 20% of probability and give yet another average, CAD 9,750. The exact tail-size convention matters. Acerbi and Tasche’s expected-shortfall paper discusses why definitions require care when a distribution has probability masses rather than a continuous spread of values.

05

A signed loss quantile can be negative while serious loss states remain

At the 80% level, cumulative probability reaches 80% at a loss of negative CAD 5,000. Under the stated inverse-cumulative convention, VaR is therefore −CAD 5,000. The calculator does not replace it with zero.

That negative loss value corresponds to a gain. It does not remove the remaining 20% of probability, which still contains losses of CAD 5,000, CAD 20,000 and CAD 40,000.

The average of that worst 20% is CAD 9,750 in the default distribution. The signed summary bars keep the negative quantile visible beside the positive tail average and largest specified loss.

Different software can use different quantile interpolation or boundary conventions. Record the loss sign, cumulative level, holding period and exact definition before comparing results from separate tools.

06

Changing the level and changing the loss states are separate operations

A higher cumulative level selects a smaller worst tail. At 99%, the defined VaR is CAD 20,000 while the worst 1% consists entirely of the CAD 40,000 outcome, so ES is CAD 40,000.

The confidence control also allows intermediate levels. Moving from 95% to 95.5% pushes the quantile past the probability jump at CAD 5,000 to CAD 20,000. The exact tail average changes from CAD 24,000 to approximately CAD 24,444.44. A discrete quantile can jump even when the tail average changes gradually.

The loss-size multiplier changes only the three loss amounts. It leaves the gain states and every probability fixed. It does not preserve the distribution’s mean or standard deviation and is not an estimate of a future stress event.

The matrix varies both the cumulative level and loss multiplier. Its cells are conditional calculations from the invented distribution. They carry no empirical probability estimates, confidence intervals or assertion that the stated worst outcome covers real-market extremes.

07

Do not turn a risk summary directly into a spending reserve

The largest loss is known here only because the model declares exactly five possible returns. An actual investment can behave outside a convenient model. Adding ES to a chart does not establish that the model’s inputs or tail coverage are reliable.

ES in this article means an average loss in a selected worst tail. It is different from the expected amount of a household budget shortfall across all states, and from the probability of missing a particular goal. Those questions need their own spending amounts, dates and resources.

Investor.gov’s risk overview discusses several risks beyond a single dispersion or loss summary. Liquidity, cash access and the consequences of a payment shortfall still matter when deciding what resources a plan can rely on.

This example includes no taxes, fees, withdrawals, repeated years, portfolio selection or regulatory-capital requirements. Use it to understand the measures and their definitions. A practical financial plan still needs evidence about the actual exposure and an independently workable cash calendar.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Four original hypothetical charts use five chosen one-year outcomes and probabilities. They do not estimate historical or future portfolio risk, use a normal distribution, calculate regulatory capital or establish a cash-reserve target. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. Acerbi, C. and Tasche, D. (2002) · On the coherence of Expected Shortfall ↗

    Public arXiv HTML v5, revised 2 May 2002; reviewed 25 October 2026. Definitions 2.1, 2.2 and 2.6 and the quantile representation explain boundary probability mass. The paper uses profit/loss and a lower-tail probability; this illustration states positive losses and the complementary cumulative confidence level. All five outcomes, probabilities and numerical calculations are original.

  2. Investor.gov · What is Risk? ↗
